newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Fed Beige Book, range trading.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Fed Beige Book, range trading.

text.p: With the Federal Reserve's Beige Book the most prominent economic release of the trading session, the U.S. government securities market is likely to trade in its current neighborhood on Wednesday, analysts said.

The Beige Book, the Fed's anecdotal account of business conditions around the nation, is expected to say what the market has already discerned -- that the economy slowed in the second quarter, economists said.
But that "news" is not likely to prod the market in either direction, they said.

"I don't expect the Beige Book to do much of anything to anybody," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "I think it's pretty clear to most people that the Fed is not going to move interest rates at the July FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting. But the market has done that trade already. To move from these levels, we need to see some data on what the economy is doing in the second half of the year."
"I think basically we're just going to be here until the next employment report," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.

The market will get revisions on first quarter productivity and unit labor costs at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Wednesday. The productivity figure is likely to come in at 2.1 percent for the first quarter, according to economists polled by Reuters. And the unit labor cost figure is expected to come in at 2.6 percent.

But analysts said first-quarter data should not affect the market. In fact, there are very few economic reports to steer prices in one direction or another until the June U.S. employment report, Feinman said.
The two reports that could be somewhat influential over the next two weeks are the weekly jobless claims figures due this Thursday and next, said Feinman.
If the jobless claims figure stays in the upper 330,000s or moves into the range of 340,000 or more, that would help the bond market, Feinman said.
But Feinman cautioned that new jobless claims on the order of 337,000 to 340,000 a week, "while higher than what we saw in the first quarter, still suggest that the economy is growing above trend."

The first half of the year saw Gross Domestic Product grow at an average rate of about 3.5 percent, Feinman said, with most of the growth occurring in the first quarter. After that, consumer spending had to pause.

"But the question is what will the consumer do in the second half of the year," said Feinman. "Economic growth won't be as strong in the second half of the year as it was in the first, but it could still be close to three percent."
With questions about the economy in the second half of the year unanswerable at this point, the market should stay in its current ranges, Rupert.

"We saw some corrective profit-taking on Tuesday and we could see a little followthrough on that early Wednesday," said Rupert. "But we should see two-way flows for the rest of the week with buyers coming in on downticks because the market is in a pretty bullish mood.
"If anything, the Fed's Beige Book has the potential to be somewhat friendly to the bond market," she added.
Rupert said the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield would encounter resistance at 6.70 percent, at 6.675 percent, and from there at 6.625 percent.
Support for the bond yield lies at 6.73 percent and then at 6.75 percent, she said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-23/32 on Tuesday, down 12/32, its yield ending at 6.72 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-5/8 percent and 5-11/16 percent on Wednesday.
